identity.title: Reflective Practice (academic skills pathway)
identity.agentDefinition: Reflective Practice is one of thirteen academic skills pathways: reflection taught as a discipline a student can do on purpose, from a three-stage cycle to the fuller models used in assessed vocational reflection and continuing professional development. Reach for it to place, sequence or assess a reflective capability, or to translate one into its workplace form. It is not a theory of reflection: Gibbs, Schön, Johns and Kolb have their own documents, and reflection on one's own learning process belongs to the pathway on learning, assessment and feedback.
identity.summary: The academic skills pathways model (2026) sets Reflective Practice as one of thirteen pathways, drawn from the treatment of reflection in a study skills guide for undergraduates and from the reflective models used in the professions. It climbs in three tiers: what reflection is and why it matters (a three-stage cycle; honest, balanced reflection); structured, critical reflection turned into action; and reflection as professional practice, using fuller models such as Gibbs, Kolb and Johns, assessed in nursing, teaching and social work, with reflexivity (examining how one's personal identity, values, assumptions and social position shape one's reflections, judgements and actions), and as continuing professional development (CPD). Its main use is as the method under other pathways: feedback, reflective writing, group work and work-based learning. Its open questions are about coverage, not a scholarly dispute: the proposed capabilities cover the tiers unevenly, and the three-stage cycle's first stage is named two ways (Part E).

levels.context: a learner entering higher education: level 3 study, access and foundation years
skills: describe an experience, what happened and how one felt
say what went well and what did not
competencies: completes a short reflection on a well-defined task with guidance
understandings: reflection is learning from experience, not only recounting it
for own development: noticing how one learns is the first step in taking charge of it
literacies: a short first-person account, mostly descriptive writing

metacognition.statement: Reflects because the task asks for it; sees reflection as something to complete, and is not yet aware of how they learn.

levels.context: the first year of higher education
skills: use a simple cycle (experience, reflect, act) on own learning and feedback
competencies: reflects on assessed work and feedback with some guidance and acts on it
understandings: reflection is part of self-regulated learning: the evaluation that feeds the next plan
for own development: reflection closes the loop from feedback to the next piece of work, so the learner steers their own improvement
literacies: a reflective journal or learning log; descriptive reflection, with reasons in plain language

metacognition.statement: Knows why reflection is asked for and begins to notice their own learning habits; still reflects mainly when prompted.

levels.changesFromBelow: from recounting to giving reasons and planning the next step, applied to one's own study

levels.context: developing practice, depending on the student: the second year, work placements
skills: reflect critically on own performance in real tasks such as group work and feedback, rather than describe it
use a recognised model such as Gibbs's cycle
turn reflection into an action plan with measurable steps
competencies: identifies own learning needs and acts on them without prompting
understandings: the same event can be read from more than one point of view
theory and literature can explain one's experience
reflective practice can evolve a practitioner identity, the move towards reflection as professional practice at level 6 (Abbott, D-ing-0035)
for own development: reflection over time makes one's growth visible and plannable across a whole course
literacies: a structured reflective essay or report linking experience to literature; dialogic reflection: stepping back, weighing alternatives

metacognition.statement: Invests in reflection, beginning to choose when and how to reflect, aware that reflection shapes who they are becoming as a practitioner; can say what the practice does for them.

levels.changesFromBelow: from one's own reasons to alternatives, other perspectives and the literature; from a next step to a plan; the first sense of reflection shaping who one is becoming as a practitioner

levels.context: independent practice: the final undergraduate year, professional placements
skills: choose and justify a reflective model for the purpose (Kolb, Gibbs, Johns)
reflect in and on action in practice settings
examine how one's own values and assumptions shape judgement (reflexivity begins)
competencies: reflects routinely as professional practice and records it as continuing professional development against a profession's standards
understandings: reflection is a professional duty in many fields, assessed against standards
personal position affects what one notices and how one judges
for own development: reflection records and directs one's continuing professional development and readiness for practice
literacies: an assessed reflective account in a vocational genre (nursing, teaching, social work); a CPD record; critical reflection placing practice in its wider context

metacognition.statement: Has made reflection their own: reflects habitually and with confidence, judges which model fits, and knows how their own position colours what they notice.

levels.changesFromBelow: from structured reflection on study to reflection as professional practice, judged against standards, with reflexivity

levels.context: advanced practice: master's study, professional development and recognition
skills: critically evaluate own and others' practice against theory and evidence
competencies: sustains reflexivity across a body of work; reflects on own progress as a learner and on professional responsibility, integrity and ethics
understandings: reflective practice is itself contested: its models, frames and power relations can be critiqued
for own development: reflecting on one's progress as a learner and practitioner sustains lifelong development and professional recognition
literacies: a reflective commentary within practice-based research; a portfolio for professional recognition

metacognition.statement: Moulds reflection to personal and professional goals and settings, combining or inventing approaches; communicates their reflection to colleagues and uses it to develop others.

levels.changesFromBelow: from reflecting on practice to critiquing practice and the frames used to reflect on it

levels.context: doctoral practice: an original contribution to knowledge, the researcher's identity and independence
skills: write a reflexive account of one's position in relation to the research
reflect on the research process and its decisions as it unfolds
plan one's development as a researcher
competencies: uses reflexivity as part of research method, so that the account of the knowledge made includes the maker
manages own development and career as a researcher
understandings: the researcher's identity, values and position shape what counts as knowledge in the study
reflection here concerns the production of knowledge, not only the improvement of practice
for own development: reflexivity shapes one's identity, independence and career as a researcher
literacies: a positionality statement and a reflexive methodology section in a thesis; a development record against a researcher framework

metacognition.statement: Reflection has become a mode of doing and expression, fluent and largely tacit, like an athlete in the flow; reflexivity is how they make and communicate knowledge in the service of their disciplinary community, and an expression of their commitment to it.

levels.changesFromBelow: a different kind, not more of level 7: reflection turns on the making of original knowledge and on the researcher's own identity and independence

theorySpine.overview:
- A pathway is defined by three tiers, Introductory, Intermediate and Advanced, each with a focus, its content, a progression logic and links to other pathways (D:PTM, Pathway 10).
- Reflection is treated as a professional discipline, formal, assessed and career-long, and kept apart from the self-regulation of learning, which another pathway holds (D:PTM, Pathway 10).
- Tiers are anchored to experience of the practice, not to year or level of study: a student may be advanced in one practice and introductory in another (D:TSPEC, section 2).
- It replaced nothing: it became a pathway of its own when the model grew from nine pathways to thirteen (D:PTM, changes, v2).
theorySpine.corePrinciples:
- A learner's development, and in the end their development into a graduate, is driven by self-reflection (D:EAU, p. 53).
- A simple three-stage cycle (describe, reflect, take action) is enough to start; assessed reflection may require a fuller model such as Kolb's or Gibbs's (D:EAU, p. 53).
- Reflection should begin with what went well and is never wholly positive or negative; starting from the positives sets a balanced tone (D:EAU, p. 54).
- The action stage turns reflection into practical steps and is the stage students most often neglect (D:EAU, p. 54).
- Reflective writing must still be critical: describing an experience without critiquing one's own actions is the common fault (D:EAU, p. 161).
- Reflective writing is a genre of its own: less formal, in the first person, focused on experience and the self rather than the discourse, so it usually needs no academic references; it is structured by a reflective cycle and ends in action (D:EAU, pp. 161-163). This pathway teaches it; Academic Writing refers to it (D-ing-0022 (b)). It also teaches the professional-practice reflective report: reflection written in report format, under headings, moving from description to analysis of what worked and what was challenging to an action plan (D-ing-0044; editorial, after Gibbs, 1988).
- Constructive reflection on performance is central to CPD and lifelong learning in professional life (D:EAU, pp. 54-55).
- In practice- and work-based learning, reflective practice is the most common form of assessment (D:EAU, p. 225).
- The pathway's progression is: what reflection is, then structured critical reflection, then professional reflective practice (D:PTM, Pathway 10).
theorySpine.selection: Choose this pathway when the aim is reflection as a deliberate, assessable practice. For reflection on one's own learning process, choose `path:understanding-learning-assessment-feedback`; for learning from placements, `path:work-based-experiential-learning`, which uses this pathway as its method. It suits badly a learner who needs one theory explained in depth: use that theory's document.

gaps.coreOpenQuestions:
1. **P2 triggers:** 4 (the external frameworks rest on web and professional sources only) and 5 (all of them read by summary). The A10 crosswalk is editorial and quotes nothing until each is read direct.
2. **Levels:** every capability's `level` is `unknown`. The model ties tiers to experience, not to level, and no source sets an FHEQ level per capability. Settled for every pathway document: `unknown`, with this reason, until a source sets a level (D-ing-0001 (a), Abbott, 21:13).
3. **Capability coverage:** settled. Four capabilities added by the model's author (D-ing-0004 (a), amended, Abbott, 21:29): two Intermediate (critical reflection; a dated action plan) and two Advanced (choosing a fuller model; reflexivity, Advanced only). They are proposed here with temporary ids (c1 to c4) until the model numbers them; the model's own capability list and tier text do not yet show them. [Added 06:37, D-ing-0045: a fifth, c5, Intermediate: the professional-practice reflective report.]
4. **The ERA cycle** has no ingestion document; D:EAU credits it to Jasper (2013) and calls it close to Driscoll (2007) (W-0001).
5. **Conflict:** the HCPC standard on reflection is numbered 10 in one source (AEP guidance, 2026) and 11 in another (AEP resource page, undated, likely the 2015 standards). Both recorded; not settled (W-0002).
6. **The first stage is named two ways:** "describe" (D:EAU, p. 53) and "Experience" (D:EAU, p. 161), the second following Jasper's ERA. Settled: Experience is preferred, describe admitted, so the ERA name holds (D-ing-0002 (a), Abbott, 21:18). The proposed capability reflective-practice/01 still says "describe"; its wording is the model's to change.
7. **Schön and Johns:** settled. The Advanced tier names its fuller models as such as Gibbs, Kolb and Johns; Schön stays a link only, as the theory behind reflective practice rather than a model a student applies (D-ing-0003 (a), Abbott, 21:26). The model's own tier text still names Gibbs and Kolb only; its wording is the model's to change.
8. **Slug:** the id is `ing:doc:pathway-reflective-practice`, not author and year, because the subject is a pathway, not a published work.
9. **Templates:** COMPOSE's GD-edu-12 (reflective account) fits Advanced; an action plan and a reflective journal entry are proposed, not in COMPOSE's catalogue.
10. **Source map:** what *Excelling at University* teaches for each capability, with pages and extracts, belongs in its guide map (held by `path`, draft), not here; the page citations here are only the provenance of claims.
11. **Progression by level (A11):** drafted 02:27 (J-ing-0001; META D-0205). Every level was read by summary only (W-0031 to W-0035); the entries are editorial readings of the descriptors and of Moon's four types of reflective writing. Moon and Bolton are recommended by META's nts as the key theory (Moon key, Bolton beside); not yet ruled, and A9 does not link them. [Ruled 02:43, D-ing-0037 (a): Moon key, Bolton beside, both in A9 and queued at META's ing; Kolb, Gibbs, Johns and Schön stay as the models the tiers teach.] Level 3 uses CQFW's numbering (RQF in England).
12. **The reflective report:** settled (D-ing-0044, Abbott, 06:19): this pathway teaches the professional-practice reflective report, reflection written in typical report format, so report writing is taught here as well as in Researching and Research Methods (research and laboratory report) and Work-Based and Experiential Learning (a context-defined lesson); Academic Writing refers to all three. The example structure (editorial, after Gibbs, 1988, as headings in the Edinburgh Reflection Toolkit and York's Skills Guides): 1 Introduction (the setting, the role and the report's purpose); 2 Description (what happened, factually); 3 Evaluation (what worked and what was challenging, positives first, following the guide's advice at p. 54); 4 Analysis (why, drawing on theory and literature); 5 Conclusion (what was learned, what skills to develop); 6 Action plan (what will be done differently, how and by when); references. Gibbs's feelings stage is folded into description and evaluation. It maps to the ERA cycle: Experience is the description, Reflect the evaluation, analysis and conclusion, Take action the action plan. The guide teaches reflective writing in essay form (pp. 161-163), not in report form. Capability: `reflective-practice/c5`, Intermediate, "Write a professional-practice reflective report in report format" (D-ing-0045, Abbott, 06:37) [was owed, 06:19 to 06:37]. A published study-skills treatment to read direct: W-0053.
13. **Vocabulary (D-ing-0050, Abbott, 11:10):** swept. usage.label: Courses

usage.label: Voice band
usage.text: Default anchor, bands 2 to 4: Introductory takes the voice specification's Beginner band, Intermediate its Intermediate band, Advanced its Advanced band (`pathway-tier-mapping.md`, Pathway 10; tier specification section 3). This sets register, sentence length and outcome verbs.

usage.label: Outcome verbs
usage.text: Drawn from the anchored band of `reference/excelling-voice-specification.md` section 16 (tier specification section 6): Introductory from Beginner (describe, identify, recognise, explain, distinguish and so on), never evaluate or critique; Intermediate from Intermediate; Advanced from Advanced. Moved here from the core's B5 because the bands are ADAPT's.

usage.label: Reflective prompt in every lesson
usage.text: ADAPT's pedagogy log, P11 (Schön, 1983), "in use": a reflective prompt in every lesson; that it is always shell, with a subject angle, is proposed, not ruled (log D2). P12 (Gibbs, 1988) is "to consider" as a structure for the prompts; question T2 asks whether prompts should follow a named cycle (`docs/design/pedagogy-log.md`). This is why the core links Schön though the tiers do not name him.

usage.label: Benchmark mapping
usage.text: The term list's patterns are a word test: a QAA benchmark statement whose extract matches a pattern is tagged `direct` for this pathway, otherwise `indirect` (QV-TAG-2 part (e); rules v1.2 to come). The core uses the same patterns only as entry terms.

usage.label: Practice connection
usage.text: The capabilities' student-facing statements fill the opening and closing wrappers of each course, filtered by tier (D-0047; RJ-0050, held on D-0058).

usage.label: Summative parity
usage.text: The end-of-tier summative is calibrated to the tier specification section 7 row; parity holds across contexts within a pathway and tier, not across pathways.

usage.label: Vocational packs
usage.text: The pathway serves nursing, teaching and social work heavily and needs authored, discipline-aware examples beyond the book (`pathway-tier-mapping.md`, cross-cutting notes); those packs are Phase D work.
